title: How to Stop a Data Centre in Australia
content:
Resources gathered by The Commons librarians to support local communities organising and campaigning against AI Data Centres. It was initially put together to inform participants at the Community Summit in Naarm/Melbourne on 5 September 2026.

It can be daunting to go up against entrenched government and corporate power – but people power can prevail!

Here in Australia we can learn from the history of community activism in this country, as well as struggles and innovations overseas. We don’t need to reinvent the wheel. We can learn together and share lessons as campaigns evolve.

This guide is a work in progress. It builds on our international resource, How to Stop a Data Centre: Tools for Community Resistance. We welcome feedback and suggestions for inclusion: Contact us.

From past experience and the expressed needs of people involved in these fights, we believe the following areas of knowledge and skills are crucial.

  • Know about Data Centres
  • Know about the specific Data Centre project you want to stop 
  • Engage the Community 
  • Organise Locally 
  • Plan a Strategic Campaign
  • Tell the Story
  • Take Action 
  • Reflect and Adapt 
  • Collaborate Across the Movement

title: Talking When We Disagree – Download Free Guide
content:
It starts with having better conversations.

Many of us have experienced conversations that quickly become tense, or we have avoided them altogether for fear of conflict, misunderstanding or damaging a relationship. But social change has always depended on people being able to build relationships, listen deeply and engage with those who do not see the world the same way they do.

This guide brings together some of our favourite Commons Library resources on navigating difficult conversations, building unlikely coalitions and strengthening solidarity in divided times. Whether you are looking for practical conversation techniques, examples of deep canvassing or lessons from movements that have successfully organised across difference, these resources offer both inspiration and practical tools.

Sign up to The Commons Social Change Library newsletter to get your free guide – Talking When We Disagree: How to Talk about Sensitive Topics, featuring practical tools for navigating disagreement, building understanding and organising across difference.
snippet: It starts with having better conversations.

title: Striking Voices: Young People and Climate Justice
content:
The Striking Voices project is a transgenerational participatory project about climate justice, young people’s collective advocacy, and the role of education in times of escalating, overlapping injustices.

This four year project (2022-2026), with four younger climate justice organisers employed as Research Associates, has involved storytelling and creative-making processes, with other young (12-24 years old) climate justice organisers, their mentors, and secondary school teachers, about their experiences of climate justice activism/advocacy/organising and education.

The project has been funded by the Australian Research Council (DE220100103; 2022-2026) and Deakin University.

title: Funny Climate Activism? An Analysis of Creative Digital Action by Young People
content:
The following is a summary and excerpts from the article ‘Funny climate activism? A collaborative storied analysis of young climate advocates’ digital activisms’. It was originally published in the journal Global Studies of Childhood in 2024 and was written by Sophie Chiew, Eve Mayes, Netta Maiava, Dani Villafaña and Natasha Abhayawickrama. These five researchers are associated with Striking Voices, a participatory research project exploring how young people in Australia use activism, creative storytelling, and education to fight for climate justice. Four of the authors are 19 to 22 years old and involved in climate justice organizing and one is a university-based researcher in their early 40s.

In the face of intersecting injustices, humour has the potential to enliven and sustain collective solidarity. Collective work towards climate justice feels good when ‘wacky’ actions are done together, stereotypes and affinities are laughed at… and false forms of liberation… are satirised. – Chiew, Mayes, Maiava, Villafaña and Abhayawickrama, 2024

title: Young People, Climate Justice and Curriculum Justice
content:
This article was first published on The Curriculum Journal, BERA and is an output from the Striking Voices research project.

While many agree that education is essential to prepare societies to address the climate crisis, there are widely differing opportunities for justice-driven climate change education (see Trott et al., 2023) that centres the intersecting social injustices that climate change amplifies and compounds (Sultana, 2022).

If the purpose of education is to transform the world, it is time to centre justice, equity and solidarity in school-based climate change education.

If the purpose of education is to transform the world, it is time to centre justice, equity and solidarity in school-based climate change education.

In this post, we share how young climate justice advocates in Australia narrate their experiences of learning (or not) about climate change and justice within and beyond mainstream schooling.

title: Democratic Decision Making within your Organisation
content:
An excerpt about democratic decision making and mapping authority within your organisation from AORTA – Anti Oppression Resource and Training Alliance.

In order to shift how we govern, we must first understand how decisions are currently made. Many groups never get around to writing down who has authority over what decisions, and we get why.

Writing down the nuts and bolts of decision making can feel both tedious and intimidating! But when there is no map, it’s easy for authority and information to accumulate in inequitable ways over time without anyone realizing it. Often, the people who have the most understanding of how decisions are made are also the people who have the most power, leaving people who have less power in the dark.

What to Try
Build a map of the key decisions that the group makes. Include who makes each decision, who influences each decision, and how each decision is made. Make sure everyone in the organization understands the map.

title: The Importance of Strategic Planning in Nonviolent Struggle
content:
Chapter 2 of There Are Realistic Alternatives by Gene Sharp.

The use of strategy is best known in military conflict. For centuries military officers have engaged in strategic planning for military campaigns, and important thinkers such as Sun Tzu, Clausewitz, and Liddell Hart have analyzed and refined military strategy. In conventional military warfare and in guerrilla warfare, the use of sophisticated strategy is a basic requirement for effectiveness.
Just as effective military struggle requires wise strategies, planning, and implementation, nonviolent action will be most effective
when it also operates on the basis of sound strategic planning. The formulation and adoption of wise strategies can greatly increase the power of nonviolent struggle.

If one wishes to accomplish something, the chances of achieving that goal will be greatest if one uses one’s available resources and leverage to maximum effectiveness. That means having a strategic plan that is designed to move from the present (in which the goal is not achieved) to the future (in which it is achieved).

title: Steps in Strategic Planning for Nonviolent Struggles against Repressive Regimes
content:
Chapter 3 of There Are Realistic Alternatives by Gene Sharp.

Nonviolent struggle is a technique for conducting conflicts by social, psychological, economic, and political methods of protest, noncooperation, and disruptive intervention.

It is a technique built on the social, economic, and political application of basic human stubbornness—the determination and ability to dissent, to refuse to cooperate, to defy, and to disrupt. In other words, people may refuse to do things they are asked to do, and may do what they are forbidden to do.

All governments rely on cooperation and obedience for their very existence. When people choose to withhold or withdraw that cooperation, governments are left without any pillars to support their weight.

All governments rely on cooperation and obedience for their very existence. When people choose to withhold or withdraw that cooperation, governments are left without any pillars to support their weight.

Nonviolent struggle has been applied in various types of conflicts throughout human history to resist oppression, undermine
dictatorships, oppose foreign occupations, defend detested minorities, and to expand freedom.

title: Where to Find Social Movement Research
content:
Want to access the latest research into social change and activism? We’ve rounded up some of the best sources of social movement research around the world, including research hubs, networks, academic journals, blogs and magazines. Here you’ll find the latest insights into how social change happens, political analysis, and tips for evidence-based advocacy.

Advocacy Research Network
Advocacy Research Network is a network of researchers in Australia providing targeted intelligence to help advocacy organisations build stronger campaigns and achieve their goals. Some of their services include: target research, community mapping, strategic intelligence, policy & impact analysis, data analysis and monitoring, and movement research.

Australian Policy Online – See Subjects – Activism and Protests Movements
APO is an open access evidence platform – making public policy research and resources accessible and useable.
You can narrow results to “activism” and “protest movements” to find relevant research and reporting. 
Note that you’ll find reports from a range of sources here, be sure to check and acknowledge the source.

title: The Elements of Mutual Aid Series
content:
This series gathers the voices of community organizers who are tending grassroots alternatives to systems of oppression. Weaving together over 60 voices and profiling 15 groups across North America, the series explores the radical values, infrastructure, healing ways and logistics of mutual aid work.

The Elements of Mutual Aid is a four-part series. Each hour-long chapter represents a different theme, which are depicted through the four natural elements:

  • Chapter 1: Fire explores the history and values of liberatory mutual aid
  • Chapter 2: Earth focuses on building and networking communal infrastructure
  • Chapter 3: Water discusses healing from oppression and healing our communities
  • Chapter 4: Air delves into the logistics of non-hierarchical organizing

    • This series was made to be a tool for community learning and reflective, strategy-building conversations. We have to figure out how to transform our mutual aid efforts into deeply relational, strategic, and revolutionary practices, and we have to take time to figure out how do to that together. Source
